prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Every dog has his day, but Sir Lancelot -- or at least his carbon copy -- has a second one. Edgar and Nina Otto show off 10-week-old Lancey, a clone of "the most human of any dog we've ever had." A Boca Raton, Florida, couple paid a California firm $155,000 to clone their beloved Labrador retriever, who died from cancer a year ago. The clone, a 10-week-old puppy dubbed Lancey, was hand-delivered to them earlier this week by Lou Hawthorne, chairman of BioArts International, a biotechnology company. "One minute with Lancey and you know he's special. He's both extremely aware and very sweet," Hawthorne said in a BioArts statement. Edgar and Nina Otto said they began thinking about cloning Sir Lancelot about five years ago. "I said 'Well, you know, it wouldn't hurt to have his DNA frozen,' and that's what we did," Nina Otto told CNN affiliate WPBF. The Ottos were one of five families to bid and win a BioArts auction for a chance to clone their family dog, according to a BioArts statement. Lancey is the world's first commercially cloned dog, the company said; the Ottos are the first of six current clients to receive their clone. Sir Lancelot's DNA sample was sent to the Sooam Biotech Research Foundation in Seoul, South Korea, which provides cloning services to BioArts. Researchers there put the DNA into an egg, and Lancey was born November 18, according to BioArts. The Ottos said they have had many beloved dogs over the years -- and have nine others currently -- but maintain Sir Lancelot was special. "Sir Lancelot was the most human of any dog we've ever had," Edgar Otto said in the BioArts statement. "He was a prince among dogs." In an interview with WPBF, Edgar Otto said Sir Lancelot "was a very, very, very special dog to us. And we've given a lot more to the Humane Society than we've ever spent on this project."  Watch the Ottos talk about Lancelot and Lancey » . For its part, the Humane Society of the United States says it's against the commercial cloning of animals. "Given the current pet overpopulation problem, which costs millions of animals their lives and millions in public tax dollars each year, the cloning of pets has no social value and in fact may lead to increased animal suffering," the organization said on its Web site. "For those looking to replace a lost pet, cloning will not create an animal identical to the one who is gone; cloning cannot replicate an animal's uniqueness. Cloning can only replicate the pet's genetics, which influence but do not determine his physical attributes or personality." The Ottos, however, said replicating Sir Lancelot's genetics is enough for them. Edgar Otto said he realizes Lancey might not be just like their departed dog, but "if he's different, we're not going to love him any less." Edgar Otto is the son of the late Edwin Otto, who was part of the founding of NASCAR and a "motorsports pioneer," according to www.ottomotorsports.com.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Sir Lancelot may be gone, but a genetic duplicate of the beloved dog has given him something of a second life.

Edgar and Nina Otto of Boca Raton, Florida, recently welcomed Lancey, a 10-week-old clone of the Labrador retriever they described as more humanlike than any dog they had ever owned. Sir Lancelot died of cancer a year earlier.

The couple paid a California company $155,000 for the cloning procedure. Lou Hawthorne, chairman of biotechnology firm BioArts International, personally delivered the puppy to the Ottos earlier this week.

After meeting Lancey, Hawthorne described him in a company statement as unusually perceptive, gentle and clearly remarkable.

The Ottos first considered cloning Sir Lancelot roughly five years ago. Nina Otto told CNN affiliate WPBF that she suggested preserving the dog’s DNA because there seemed to be no harm in doing so, and the couple subsequently had a sample frozen.

According to BioArts, the Ottos were among five families that submitted successful bids in an auction offering the opportunity to clone a household dog. The company called Lancey the first dog in the world to be cloned commercially. It also said the Ottos were the first of its six existing clients to take possession of their cloned pet.

Sir Lancelot’s genetic material was shipped to the Sooam Biotech Research Foundation in Seoul, South Korea, which performs cloning work for BioArts. Scientists inserted the DNA into an egg, and Lancey was born on November 18, the company said.

Although the Ottos have loved many dogs over the years—and currently own nine others—they said Sir Lancelot stood apart. In the BioArts statement, Edgar Otto characterized him as the most humanlike dog they had ever known and called him royalty among canines.

Speaking with WPBF, Edgar Otto repeatedly emphasized how important Sir Lancelot had been to the family. He also said the couple had donated far more money to the Humane Society than they spent on the cloning effort.

Watch the Ottos discuss Sir Lancelot and Lancey.

The Humane Society of the United States, however, opposes cloning animals for commercial purposes. On its website, the organization argued that cloning pets offers no benefit to society and could worsen animal suffering, particularly when pet overpopulation already results in the deaths of millions of animals and costs taxpayers millions of dollars annually.

The group also warned that cloning cannot produce an exact replacement for a deceased pet. While the process can duplicate an animal’s genes, it cannot reproduce the individual qualities that made the original animal unique. Genetics may affect appearance and temperament, the organization said, but they do not fully determine either.

For the Ottos, reproducing Sir Lancelot’s genetic makeup was sufficient. Edgar Otto acknowledged that Lancey may not grow up to be exactly like the dog they lost, but said any differences would not diminish the family’s love for him.

Edgar Otto is the son of the late Edwin Otto, who helped establish NASCAR and is described by OttoMotorsports.com as a pioneer in motor racing.
outputs.L3:
Edgar and Nina Otto paid $155,000 to clone their beloved Labrador retriever, Sir Lancelot, after he died from cancer. The Florida couple had preserved the dog’s DNA, hoping it could one day be used to create a genetic copy.

The preserved DNA was sent to the Sooam Biotech Research Foundation in South Korea, where scientists inserted it into an egg as part of the cloning process. The resulting puppy was born on November 18 and named Lancey. At 10 weeks old, Lancey was delivered to the Ottos by BioArts International, the company that arranged the procedure.

BioArts described Lancey as the world’s first commercially cloned dog. The Ottos were among five families that secured the opportunity to clone a pet through an auction organized by the company. They said they chose to proceed because they considered Sir Lancelot an exceptionally special dog.

Commercial pet cloning remains controversial, however. While the Ottos viewed the procedure as a way to preserve a connection to their cherished companion, the Humane Society of the United States opposes commercial animal cloning, citing ethical and animal-welfare concerns.
outputs.L4:
A Florida couple, Nina and Edgar Otto, paid $155,000 to have their deceased Labrador retriever, Sir Lancelot, cloned. Before the dog died, the Ottos had preserved some of his cells, hoping that advances in biotechnology might one day allow them to create a genetic copy of their beloved pet.

The procedure was arranged by the California-based company BioArts International and carried out by researchers in South Korea. Scientists transferred genetic material from Sir Lancelot’s preserved cells into an egg whose nucleus had been removed. The resulting embryo was then implanted into a surrogate dog, which gave birth to a healthy yellow Labrador puppy. The Ottos named him Lancelot Encore, or “Lancey.”

Lancey was described as the world’s first commercially cloned dog because he was produced for a private customer through a paid cloning service. His birth represented an important milestone in animal biotechnology and demonstrated that pet cloning, once largely experimental, could be offered commercially to owners willing to pay a substantial price.

The achievement also generated controversy. Animal-welfare organizations argued that cloning is costly, inefficient and potentially harmful because it may require numerous eggs, embryos and surrogate animals to produce a single healthy puppy. Critics also noted that shelters contain many dogs in need of homes. Supporters, however, viewed Lancey’s birth as a scientific breakthrough and a deeply personal way for the Ottos to preserve Sir Lancelot’s genetic legacy. Although Lancey was genetically almost identical to the original Labrador, his personality and behavior would still be shaped by his own experiences and environment.
